title: Cómo acompañar emocionalmente a una persona después de una emergencia: guía para familiares, amigos y voluntarios
summary: Cómo acompañar emocionalmente a alguien después de una emergencia: qué decir, cómo escuchar y qué frases evitar. Guía para familiares y voluntarios.
body_text: En Resumen Lo que encontrarás en este artículo: Qué significa realmente acompañar (y qué no es) Cómo escuchar de forma que la persona se sienta comprendida Qué frases evitar porque minimizan lo que el otro vive Cómo respetar los límites y cuidarte tú también ‍ Acompañar no es solucionar El primer cambio de mirada es el más importante: acompañar no es arreglar. Ante el dolor de otro, sentimos la urgencia de "hacer algo" para que deje de sufrir, y esa urgencia nos empuja a dar consejos, buscar el lado positivo o minimizar el problema. Con buena intención, pero muchas veces eso deja a la persona más sola. Lo que la mayoría necesita después de una emergencia no es una solución, sino sentirse acompañada en lo que siente. Saber que su dolor es válido, que puede estar mal sin que alguien intente convencerla de lo contrario, que hay alguien dispuesto a quedarse. Acompañar es sostener sin apurar. Es transmitir, con tu presencia: "estoy aquí, no me voy a ir aunque no tenga la respuesta". Muchas veces, ese es el apoyo más valioso que existe. El arte de escuchar Escuchar de verdad es más difícil de lo que parece, porque implica callar nuestra necesidad de responder. Escuchar bien es dejar que la persona hable a su ritmo, sin interrumpir, sin corregir su forma de sentir, sin saltar a dar tu opinión. Practica la escucha con el cuerpo: mira a los ojos, asiente, deja silencios. No hace falta llenar cada pausa con palabras. A veces un "aquí estoy" y una presencia serena dicen más que cualquier discurso. Si la persona no quiere hablar, respétalo; estar en silencio a su lado también es acompañar. En la experiencia de los terapeutas de Selia, lo que más contiene a alguien en crisis no es el consejo brillante, sino sentirse verdaderamente escuchado. Ser escuchado sin juicio es, en sí mismo, reparador. ‍ ¿Qué decir para que la persona se sienta comprendida? Las mejores palabras suelen ser sencillas y honestas. Validan en lugar de aconsejar, acompañan en lugar de empujar. Puedes decir cosas como "lamento mucho lo que estás viviendo", "estoy aquí contigo", "tiene sentido que te sientas así", o "no tienes que pasar por esto solo". Preguntar en vez de asumir también ayuda mucho: "¿cómo te puedo ayudar hoy?", "¿quieres hablar o prefieres que te acompañe en silencio?". Devolverle a la persona algo de elección le regresa una sensación de control que la emergencia le quitó. Y si no sabes qué decir, sé honesto: "no sé qué decir, pero me importas y estoy aquí". La sinceridad conecta más que cualquier frase ensayada. No tienes que iluminar la oscuridad del otro; basta con no dejarlo a oscuras solo. ¿Alguien cercano atraviesa el impacto de una emergencia? Conoce cómo Selia puede acompañarlo → Frases que conviene evitar Algunas frases, aunque bienintencionadas, minimizan lo que la persona siente y la hacen sentir incomprendida. "Todo pasa por algo", "al menos estás vivo", "podría haber sido peor", "ya deberías estar mejor", "no es para tanto". Todas comunican, sin querer, que su dolor está de más. Evita también comparar con tu propia experiencia ("a mí me pasó algo peor"), apurar el proceso, o dar consejos que no te pidieron sobre qué debería hacer. Y cuida el impulso de hablar más de tus emociones que de las suyas: este es su momento. En lugar de forzar el lado positivo, quédate en la validación. Cambia el "no llores" por "llora lo que necesites, aquí estoy". Ese simple giro transforma el acompañamiento. Si acompañas a alguien tras un desastre en particular, puedes profundizar en nuestra guía sobre primeros auxilios psicológicos después de un sismo . Respetar límites y cuidarte tú Acompañar bien también es respetar los tiempos y los límites del otro. No todas las personas procesan igual: algunas necesitan hablar mucho, otras silencio; algunas quieren compañía constante, otras momentos a solas. Sigue su ritmo, sin presionar ni desaparecer, y sostén la relación también en las semanas siguientes, cuando la atención de todos baja. Y no olvides cuidarte a ti. Acompañar el dolor ajeno cansa, y sostener a otros sin descanso lleva al agotamiento. Pon límites sanos, tómate pausas, apóyate en más personas y no cargues solo. Un acompañante cuidado tiene mucho más para dar. Si notas que, con el tiempo, la persona no logra recuperarse o su malestar se profundiza, anímala con cariño a buscar ayuda profesional. Reconocer cuándo hace falta más que tu apoyo es también una forma de cuidarla. Preguntas Frecuentes ¿Qué hago si la persona no quiere hablar de lo que le pasó? Respeta su silencio; no todos procesan hablando, y forzar el relato puede ser contraproducente. Puedes quedarte a su lado, ofrecerle compañía o ayuda concreta, y hacerle saber que estás disponible cuando quiera. Tu presencia serena ya es una forma de apoyo, aunque no se digan muchas palabras. ¿Cómo sé si estoy ayudando o incomodando? Observa y pregunta. Si la persona se abre, agradece tu compañía o se muestra más tranquila contigo, vas bien. Si necesita espacio, respétalo sin tomarlo como algo personal. Preguntar directamente "¿te ayuda que esté aquí o prefieres un rato a solas?" despeja la duda y le devuelve el control sobre lo que necesita. ¿Puedo acompañar a alguien si yo también estoy afectado? Sí, pero cuidándote primero. Si tú también viviste la emergencia, necesitas tu propio espacio para procesarla. Acompañar desde el agotamiento no ayuda a nadie. Reparte la carga, apóyate en otros y date permiso de ser tú quien reciba apoyo cuando lo necesites. Cuidarte no es egoísmo: es lo que te permite sostener. ¿Cuándo debo recomendarle ayuda profesional? Cuando notes que, con el paso de las semanas, el malestar no baja o empeora: insomnio persistente, angustia constante, aislamiento, incapacidad de retomar la vida o pensamientos de hacerse daño. Sugerírselo con cariño y ofrecerte a acompañar el primer paso puede marcar la diferencia. Tu apoyo y la terapia se complementan. Conclusión Acompañar emocionalmente a alguien después de una emergencia no exige tener respuestas ni palabras perfectas. Exige presencia, escucha honesta, validación y respeto por sus tiempos. Estar, incluso cuando no puedes arreglar nada. Ese acompañamiento humano es una de las formas más poderosas de cuidado que existen. Y cuando el dolor pesa demasiado, recordar que hay ayuda profesional —y ofrecerte a buscarla juntos— es otro gesto de amor. Nadie debería atravesar lo difícil en soledad. Nota importante : Este artículo tiene fines informativos y no reemplaza el consejo de un profesional de salud mental. Si la persona a la que acompañas presenta señales de crisis o riesgo, busca ayuda inmediata: en Colombia, Línea 106; en México, SAPTEL 55 5259-8121; en España, Teléfono de la Esperanza 717 003 717.

title: What Is Email Deliverability? a Complete Guide for 2026
summary: Wondering what is email deliverability and why your emails go to spam? Learn how it works, what key metrics to track, and how to improve your inbox placement.
body_text: SEO title: What Is Email Deliverability? A Complete Guide for 2026 Meta description: Learn what email deliverability is, how it differs from email delivery, why emails land in spam, and how to improve inbox placement with practical guidance. Suggested URL slug: what-is-email-deliverability Primary keyword: what is email deliverability Secondary keywords: email deliverability, inbox placement, sender reputation, email delivery vs deliverability, avoid spam folder, cold email deliverability, sender reputation monitoring Email deliverability is whether a message reaches the inbox instead of spam or another filtered folder, while email delivery only means the receiving server accepted it. A 2026 multi-ESP test found an average deliverability rate of 83.1% , which means 16.9% of emails did not reach the inbox. That gap is where a lot of email programs fail. A founder can have a solid offer, decent copy, and a clean-looking campaign report, yet still miss pipeline because the message was accepted by the server but filtered before a human ever saw it. That is why deliverability matters so much. It sits between sending and actual business impact. For sales teams, poor deliverability means fewer replies. For marketers, it means campaigns underperform even when the creative is strong. For recruiters, it means outreach gets ignored for reasons that have nothing to do with the role or message. The common problem is the same. The inbox providers do not fully trust the sender. Why Your Emails Are Landing in Spam Teams often discover deliverability only after something breaks. A campaign goes out. Results drop. Open signals weaken. Replies disappear. The natural reaction is to rewrite the subject line or change the call to action. Sometimes that helps. Often it doesn't, because the underlying issue sits one level deeper. The issue is email deliverability . A 2026 deliverability benchmark found an average deliverability rate of 83.1% , meaning 16.9% of emails did not reach the inbox. In practical terms, nearly 1 in 6 marketing emails can fail to reach the inbox even in modern sending environments. That explains why a campaign can look fine on the sending side and still fail on the receiving side. What spam placement usually looks like in practice Founders and operators usually notice deliverability problems through symptoms, not dashboards: Reply volume drops first , especially on outbound campaigns that used to perform consistently. Marketing engagement softens , even when the audience and offer haven't changed much. Recruitment outreach stalls , with qualified candidates never seeing the first touch. Transactional trust suffers , because users start missing important emails and contact support. Poor deliverability doesn't just hurt one send. It teaches mailbox providers to trust future sends less. Why this becomes a business problem fast Mailbox providers don't evaluate a campaign in isolation. They evaluate the sender over time. That means weak list quality, sudden volume spikes, broken authentication, low engagement, and spam complaints don't stay contained. They affect the reputation attached to the domain and sending setup. Once that reputation slips, inbox placement gets harder across the board. Teams that need a practical path out of that cycle usually start with the basics in a guide on how to avoid landing in spam , then move into monitoring and reputation work. What Is Email Deliverability vs Email Delivery What is email deliverability? Email deliverability is the ability of an email to land in the recipient's inbox instead of spam, quarantine, or another filtered folder. Email delivery is simpler. It only means the receiving server accepted the message. That distinction matters more than is often realized. According to Validity's explanation of email delivery and deliverability , a sender can have high delivery rates yet still poor inbox placement. A simple way to think about it Delivery is like a package reaching the building. Deliverability is whether that package makes it to the person's desk instead of getting dumped in the mailroom or flagged by security. The building accepted it. The recipient still may never see it. That is why many senders misread their own results. They see a healthy delivery metric and assume the message reached the audience. In reality, the server said yes, but the mailbox provider still filtered the email based on trust signals. Why inbox placement is the real KPI If the goal is pipeline, demos, purchases, applications, or account activity, the essential question isn't "Was the message accepted?" The important question is "Did it land where a person would notice it?" This is why inbox placement rate is the more useful operating metric for serious email teams. A practical comparison makes the difference clear: Metric What it tells you What it doesn't tell you Email delivery The receiving server accepted the message Whether it landed in inbox or spam Email deliverability The message reached the inbox instead of a filtered folder Why it was filtered without deeper diagnostics Inbox placement rate How often messages actually land in inbox The full cause unless paired with reputation and engagement data Practical rule: If a team only tracks delivery, it's measuring transport, not visibility. How Mailbox Providers Evaluate Your Sender Reputation Mailbox providers treat every sender like a reputation case. They don't inspect one message and decide. They look at patterns. Is this sender authenticated correctly? Do recipients engage with the mail? Does volume look normal? Are complaints rising? Is this domain behaving like a trusted sender or like a spam source? That is why deliverability is better understood as continuous reputation management . Authentication is now table stakes Mailbox providers have become more explicit about what they require. Mailjet's guidance on modern deliverability requirements notes that Gmail and Yahoo now require SPF and DKIM for all senders and DMARC for bulk senders , while also enforcing spam complaint rates below 0.3% . That changes the conversation. Authentication is no longer a nice technical upgrade. It is part of the trust threshold. If SPF, DKIM, or DMARC is missing or broken, the sender is asking providers to trust a message that hasn't been properly verified. That is a poor starting point. Reputation comes from behavior, not setup alone Technical setup matters, but it doesn't solve reputation by itself. Mailbox providers also watch behavioral signals such as: Recipient engagement , including whether people open, reply, or interact positively with mail Complaint signals , especially when recipients mark messages as spam Sending consistency , because sudden volume changes often look risky List quality , since stale or invalid contacts create negative outcomes quickly This is why teams can "pass authentication" and still land in spam. They handled identity, but not trust. The four signals that usually move outcomes A useful way to think about mailbox-provider evaluation is through four buckets: Reputation signal What providers infer Authentication Is this sender legitimate and properly configured? Engagement Do recipients appear to want these emails? Sending history Is this sender stable and predictable over time? List quality and content Is the sender reaching the right people with credible messages? A weak score in one area can drag the others down. For example, a clean domain with poor engagement can still lose inbox placement. A strong campaign with sloppy authentication can still be filtered. The system is cumulative. Teams that want a clearer view of how providers judge them usually need to monitor both domain health and mailbox-specific reputation signals. A practical starting point is this guide to domain reputation and mailbox trust . A sender reputation problem rarely starts with one bad email. It usually starts with repeated signals that tell providers the audience isn't responding well. How mailbox providers think Mailbox providers optimize for user trust, not sender convenience. Their job is to protect the inbox. That means they reward senders who look consistent, authenticated, and wanted. They filter senders who create uncertainty, low engagement, or complaints. Once that is understood, deliverability stops feeling random. It becomes a system. And systems can be improved when the team tracks the right inputs. Key Metrics to Track Your Deliverability If deliverability is a reputation system, it needs a scorecard. The mistake many teams make is watching only one metric. They focus on delivery rate, or they obsess over opens, or they wait until reply volume drops. None of those alone gives a reliable picture. A better approach is to monitor a small set of metrics together. According to Mailtrap's deliverability benchmarks , strong email programs typically target 95%+ inbox placement , with 98–99% delivery rates and spam complaint rates kept below 0.1% . The metrics that matter most Here is the short list worth tracking consistently: Inbox placement rate This is the most important measure of whether email is being seen. Delivery rate Useful, but incomplete. It confirms server acceptance, not inbox visibility. Spam complaint rate One of the clearest negative trust signals a sender can produce. Bounce rate High bounce patterns usually point to list quality or acquisition problems. Engagement trend Open, click, and reply patterns help indicate whether recipients want the mail. What each metric is good for Metric Best use Common mistake Inbox placement rate Measuring true visibility Ignoring it and relying only on delivery Delivery rate Checking basic transport health Treating it as proof of inboxing Spam complaints Spotting trust damage early Looking at complaints too late Bounces Diagnosing bad data and poor hygiene Assuming they are just a technical issue Engagement signals Understanding recipient interest Reading them without mailbox context A lot of teams also benefit from watching provider-level patterns. Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo, and Microsoft 365 do not always react the same way. A campaign can look healthy overall while one provider is routing a large share of mail into spam. For a quick visual walkthrough of the metrics and the logic behind them, this overview is useful: The right dashboard doesn't answer every deliverability question. It tells the team where to investigate first. What founders should actually review A busy founder does not need to become a full-time deliverability analyst. But someone on the team should review: Inbox placement by provider Complaint trends after major sends Bounce patterns by list source Engagement changes after content or volume changes Those four views usually reveal whether the issue is technical, reputational, list-related, or campaign-specific. Common Causes of Poor Email Deliverability Most deliverability failures are not mysterious. They are the cumulative result of a few predictable mistakes. Some are technical. Some are operational. Some come from pressure to grow fast. The worst outcomes usually happen when several of them stack together. Missing or broken authentication If a domain isn't properly authenticated, mailbox providers have less reason to trust its mail. That does not just affect security. It affects placement. A sender with weak authentication often sees more filtering, more doubt, and less room for error when other signals are average. Poor list quality List quality problems show up fast. Purchased lists, scraped contacts, old databases, and weak signup validation all create the same downstream damage. More bounces. More complaints. Lower engagement. More negative signals attached to the sender. A list can be large and still be low quality. That is one of the most common traps in outbound and lifecycle email. Cold sending from a fresh domain New domains and newly active mailboxes have no real trust history. If a team starts sending aggressively from a cold setup, providers often treat that behavior as suspicious. The problem isn't only volume. It's the mismatch between zero history and immediate scale. New sending environments need to earn trust before they can safely push volume. Sudden volume spikes Mailbox providers like consistency because consistency looks legitimate. A sharp jump in sending volume, especially from a sender with weak engagement or limited history, often triggers filtering. This happens when teams import a large list, launch a promotion to an untested segment, or turn on a new sequence too quickly. Low engagement and high complaints Many deliverability programs break at this stage. Even when authentication is correct and bounce rates look manageable, poor recipient response changes the reputation picture. If people ignore the mail, delete it, unsubscribe aggressively, or complain, providers learn that the sender is not creating wanted mail. Content that increases filtering risk Content usually isn't the root cause by itself, but it can make a weak reputation worse. Messages with misleading framing, heavy promotional language, cluttered formatting, or suspicious link patterns are harder to place well when the sender already has trust issues. A practical troubleshooting checklist looks like this: Check authentication first , because trust starts with verified identity Audit list sources , especially imported or older segments Review recent volume changes , including new automations or campaigns Look at complaint and engagement trends , not just aggregate performance Inspect content patterns , especially links, wording, and formatting consistency The pattern matters more than any single send. One flawed campaign can hurt. Repeated weak signals will almost always hurt. How to Improve and Monitor Your Deliverability Fixing deliverability means changing both setup and operating habits. That is where many guides fall short. They explain the basics, but they don't spend enough time on what teams should do once reputation has already weakened. Higher Logic's deliverability guidance points out that content on this topic often underexplains what senders should do when reputation is harmed by low engagement or high complaint rates, and that the biggest operational decisions now happen in pre-send testing and post-send monitoring. Start with control, not guesswork When deliverability slips, the right first move is usually to reduce variables. That means tightening the audience, slowing any risky volume changes, and checking the sender's technical foundation. Teams that haven't recently reviewed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC should fix that first, and this guide to mastering email authentication is a useful starting point. Then the team should shift into a simple operating loop: Test before large sends Review likely risks before a campaign goes live. Watch provider-level outcomes Gmail and Outlook may behave differently from the same campaign. React quickly to negative signals When engagement weakens or complaints rise, do not keep pushing the same volume. Protect the list Suppress bad data, inactive contacts, and segments that repeatedly underperform. Monitoring tools help, but they aren't enough Google Postmaster Tools, Microsoft SNDS, feedback loops, and ESP analytics all matter. They show how mailbox providers see the sender. They help spot complaint issues, reputation shifts, and provider-specific weakness. But these tools mostly show symptoms. They rarely rebuild trust by themselves. That is why many teams pair monitoring with a more active reputation strategy, including list cleanup, provider-aware sending controls, and warm-up workflows. Teams that want another practical perspective on recovery and inbox placement can also review this guide on email deliverability best practices . For teams comparing broader email deliverability strategies , it helps to evaluate whether the plan includes both diagnosis and reputation repair. What usually works and what doesn't A practical comparison is more useful than another generic checklist: Usually works Usually doesn't Fixing authentication gaps Sending more volume to "test" the issue Reducing poor-fit segments Keeping stale contacts because the list is large Gradual sending patterns Abrupt spikes from a weak sender profile Provider-level monitoring Looking only at aggregate campaign reports Pre-send testing and post-send review Treating deliverability as a one-time setup A stable deliverability program is not built through one repair. It is maintained through consistent inputs that tell providers the sender is legitimate, predictable, and wanted. The Role of Email Warm-Up and Expert Guidance Email warm-up is the process of gradually building sender reputation by increasing sending activity and generating positive engagement signals over time. That matters most when a domain is new, a mailbox is cold, or a sender is recovering from weak reputation. Warm-up does not replace authentication, list hygiene, or solid targeting. It supports them by helping providers see more normal, trusted sending behavior. Why basic warm-up is often not enough A lot of warm-up tools focus narrowly on sending automated messages back and forth. That can help at the margin, but it doesn't always give teams enough control or enough visibility into what is happening at the provider level. The deeper need is not just activity. It is credible reputation building . That usually means a combination of real engagement signals, thoughtful sending ramps, spam monitoring, and expert review when something starts going wrong. Teams evaluating outside support sometimes also compare broader email deliverability services to decide whether they need software, consulting, or both. Where Mailwarm fits Mailwarm helps teams build sender reputation with real inbox engagement. It uses 50,000+ aged real inboxes , supports opens, replies, threads, spam removal, important marking, provider-level warmup, custom content warmup, spam score monitoring, authentication fix tools, bounce prevention, inbox placement insights, deliverability analytics, and expert deliverability calls included in every plan. It also does not require IMAP access or permission to read a user's private inbox. That matters because warm-up is most useful when it is part of a broader deliverability process, not treated as a magic switch. The teams that benefit most are usually the ones that already understand the trade-off: sending more is easy, earning inbox trust is slower. The real value of expert guidance Deliverability problems often involve multiple causes at once. A team may have a complaint issue, an audience issue, and a domain setup issue at the same time. That is why expert guidance is valuable. Someone needs to separate the core cause from the surface symptom and decide what to change first. Warm-up helps. Monitoring helps. Authentication helps. But the ultimate goal is to build a system that protects sender reputation before major damage appears. Frequently Asked Questions About Email Deliverability What is email deliverability? Email deliverability is the ability of an email to reach the recipient's inbox instead of spam or another filtered folder. What is the difference between email delivery and email deliverability? Email delivery means the receiving server accepted the message. Email deliverability means the message reached the inbox. Why do emails go to spam? Common causes include weak authentication, poor list quality, low engagement, high complaint rates, sudden volume spikes, and content that increases filtering risk. Is email deliverability just a technical setup problem? No. It starts with technical setup, but mailbox providers also judge sender reputation through engagement, complaints, list quality, and sending patterns. What is a good email deliverability target? Strong programs typically aim for 95%+ inbox placement , with delivery rates of 98–99% and spam complaint rates below 0.1% . Is warm-up enough to fix deliverability? No. Warm-up can help build or rebuild sender reputation, but it does not replace authentication, list hygiene, content quality, and monitoring. How do teams monitor deliverability? ESP analytics, provider tools such as Google Postmaster Tools and Microsoft SNDS, inbox placement testing, and complaint monitoring are used. Mailwarm costs more because it combines real inbox engagement, up to 100% replies to warmup emails depending on the plan, spam score monitoring, provider-level warmup, authentication tools, no IMAP access required, and expert deliverability calls included in every plan. If email is part of the growth engine, Mailwarm helps teams build sender reputation, monitor inbox placement, and reduce spam risk with expert-guided warmup.

title: Where you can aspire to retire: UMB’s culture makes an impact
summary: We strive to hire associates who will grow their careers over the long term. Read how associates can learn, grow, succeed and belong at UMB.
body_text: The associate experience is a cornerstone of the UMB culture, where the average tenure – 8.8 years – is nearly twice the industry average ‡ . We strive to hire associates who will grow their careers at UMB over the long-term, whether that means promotions and mentoring, or career swaps to a completely different department. At UMB, you can hear from associates who have done all the above. Our goal at UMB is to create an exceptional experience – for our customers and for one another. We value diverse ideas, meaningful connections and passions that matter beyond work. To help share that message, we’ve created an associate experience manifesto: More Heart, More Trust and More Opportunity. “From the very beginning, the ‘people business’ really drew me in and continues to excite me… I have worked with many of the same people for decades, and as a result, they have become like family to me.” – Mariner Kemper, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, UMB Financial Corporation This framework is the anchor for how associates can learn, grow, succeed and belong at UMB. Beyond the ‘job’: More Heart Whether it’s having compassion for each other, our customers or our communities (or often, all of the above), associates care deeply. We support that heartfelt work through inclusive policies and empowering people to create fulfilling lives in and out of the workplace. UMB has created inclusive spaces for associates to find a sense of belonging with our Business Resource Groups (BRGs) , community and social events, leadership programs, and more. As an associate, your first day doesn’t just begin with your manager and team. Right away, you’re given opportunities to connect and mentor, opportunities to stretch your skills and your mind, and a safe atmosphere to just be you. Associate story Isabella Crabtree, client service manager in institutional custody, has been with UMB for 8 years. Since starting her family , she found support and community at UMB and now helps others do the same as an active member of the Women’s Business Resource Group (BRG). “UMB cares about our people from top to bottom and everyone in between. It shows in my own career growth. I spoke up about what I wanted, I worked for it and was supported by leadership.” – Isabella Crabtree, client service manager, institutional custody Integrity, no matter what: More Trust UMB associates work with confidence knowing that leaders and managers trust them to do the right thing no matter what. Our mission is to exceed the expectations of our customers and communities, and our core values are what connect us, distinguish us and drive us. In short, we work to live up to the highest standards—yours. You won’t see us chasing trends, and you can count on us to follow through on our long-held values, which have set us apart from our competition for more than 100 years. Associate story Erin Moran is a territory director within consumer banking, and has been with UMB for 4 years. She shows up for her team by holding herself to high standards and leading by example. “We put words into action at UMB. I had the opportunity to work with Liz Lewis (president of consumer banking and chief marketing officer) from day one. Seeing how caring and compassion she is, along with how invested she is in our team, (she) inspires me to lead in that same way.” – Erin Moran, territory director, consumer banking Built-in career growth: More Opportunity We’re committed to empowering associates to make an impact and achieve their goals through open conversations and providing the tools to develop potential. We believe effective associate development is company-provided, manager-supported and associate-driven. Our goal is to grow existing strengths and build new skills. We have well-established programs across the bank that help associates take their careers to the next level, from tuition assistance for degree programs, associate development and leadership programs , and even scholarship opportunities for the children and grandchildren of eligible associates. Each associate brings unique skills and experiences to the table, which leads to new ideas. Associates are encouraged to connect with other associates across the bank and explore different career paths at UMB. Associate story Jonathan May is a manager for the commercial credit analysis team and has been with UMB for 7 years. Throughout his career, Jonathan discovered that opportunities could come from connecting to the right people. Now, as a manager, he facilitates opportunities for his team to do the same. “As a manager, I strive to connect authentically with my team and give them an opportunity to learn and grow. Helping them build relationships is going to elevate (their) experience at work and in the community.” – Jonathan May, manager, commercial credit analysis team Count on more® with UMB At the heart of UMB is a culture that empowers associates to be a part of something more . From supporting personal journeys, doing the right thing no matter what, and developing potential by enabling growth and networking, UMB’s culture makes an impact on our associates, the company and our collective future. title: RevenueCat and AB180 partner to support South Korea’s app community
summary: RevenueCat and AB180 bring free, local-language support to South Korean app developers building and growing subscription apps.
body_text: South Korean app users are among the highest-spending mobile users in the world, with the average person spending $143 per year on apps. Now, developers in South Korea have dedicated support to capture more of that — more revenue, more retained subscribers, faster growth. We've partnered with AB180 to give South Korean developers hands-on local support and help getting the most out of RevenueCat's tools, backed by a team that already works with some of South Korea's biggest apps and games like NAVER WEBTOON, MUSINSA, Amorepacific, and Nexon. AB180 is a South Korea-based marketing technology company with over 10 years’ experience in MarTech and AdTech, and the team behind the Airbridge attribution platform. The partnership makes it easier for South Korean app developers to get local support, expert guidance, and access to world-class tools for managing and optimizing in-app subscriptions. title: The Overlooked AI Disruption in Home Financing
summary: AI-powered financial tools could automate mortgage refinancing, saving homeowners money and driving new opportunities across sectors, including housing, banking and consumer sectors.
body_text: Research The Overlooked AI Disruption in Home Financing Aug 7, 2026 The use of AI by borrowers is likely to fuel home refinancing activity, with impacts on the industry, markets and the broader economy. Key Takeaways AI adoption could boost activity in the $14 trillion U.S. residential mortgage market by an additional $2.1 trillion if mortgages rates were to rally to 5.5%. AI-powered financial tools could help homeowners capture savings and reduce the amount of time and effort to refinance mortgages, saving households a total of $4.3 billion in the rally. Increased mortgage activity could affect several sectors and markets, making AI-driven refinancing a multi-year, cross-asset investment theme. AI has the potential to automate manual origination processes, reduce costs and improve capacity, while making it easier for smaller firms to compete in the mortgage industry. Refinancing a mortgage has traditionally been a time-consuming process, requiring homeowners to research lenders, compare rates, gather documentation and complete lengthy applications. Artificial intelligence could dramatically simplify that experience—making refinancing faster, easier and more accessible for millions of borrowers. In addition to that, AI could help households find lower rates for their loans, which could lead to significant savings. Morgan Stanley Research estimates that even a modest level of AI adoption by borrowers could generate an additional $2.1 trillion in refinancing activity within the $14 trillion U.S. residential mortgage market if the mortgage rate rallied to 5.5%. "Greater volume in refinancing activities doesn’t just offer benefits to the companies enabling and supporting housing activity," says Jay Bacow, Co-Head of Securitized Products Research at Morgan Stanley., “We also expect increased efficiency in borrowing to have implications across fixed income and broader macroeconomic sectors in a multi-year, cross-asset theme.” Making Refinancing Easier for Homeowners Over the past 25 years, only about 29% of U.S. homeowners have taken advantage of opportunities to prepay or refinance their mortgages, despite potential financial benefits. Many borrowers are unaware of refinancing opportunities, lack the time to evaluate their options or are discouraged by the complexity and paperwork involved. Morgan Stanley Research estimates that AI could increase prepayment adoption from 29% annually to 60% in its base-case scenario by improving the borrower experience in several ways, including: Continuously monitoring mortgage rates and borrower eligibility Automatically preparing required documentation Personalizing and simplifying the application process Accelerating approvals and shortening closing timelines Identifying refinancing opportunities as soon as they become economically beneficial "We are imagining a world where homeowners who use AI agents to manage personal finances can automatically shop lenders for the best rate and refinance when it makes economic sense," Bacow says. "We expect to see more AI disruption in the mortgage market from consumers adopting AI to manage their finances and refinance than from originators reducing closing costs and increasing efficiencies." AI Could Also Reshape Mortgage Lending However, lenders are certainly positioned to benefit from greater AI usage as well. Today, the mortgage origination process—from receiving a loan application to the final disbursement of funds—remains highly manual and labor-intensive, with several tasks well suited to AI and automation. Increased use of AI could reduce costs, increase operational capacity and improve efficiency across the lending process. At the same time, it may lower barriers to entry for smaller lenders and increase pricing transparency for consumers, potentially putting pressure on industry margins. Fixed Income Mortgage-backed securities (MBS) investors are typically compensated for prepayment risk. If AI enables homeowners to refinance more efficiently, higher prepayment rates could reduce the relative attractiveness of MBS. More broadly, lower interest rates could increase demand for longer-duration fixed-income investments. Equities Companies that enable or benefit from increased mortgage and housing activity could see stronger growth. These include credit bureaus, banks, homebuilders, home improvement retailers and mortgage servicing firms. Housing By making mortgages easier to obtain and refinance, AI could improve access to homeownership for both existing homeowners and first-time buyers. Increased credit availability could also support higher levels of home construction and sales. Consumers Helping borrowers identify better refinancing opportunities could increase household savings and accelerate debt reduction. In Morgan Stanley Research's base-case scenario, households would save an average of $3,583 per year, generating $4.3 billion in additional annual mortgage-related savings across 1.2 million U.S. households if primary rates fall to 5.5%. Those savings could free up income for spending in home-related categories such as furniture, pet care and housekeeping supplies, while also strengthening household balance sheets. 7275232 63766 3CD19151-F46C-4595-84CF-8EEC3E05FD19 Sign up to get Morgan Stanley Ideas delivered to your inbox. title: Array Labs Raises Additional $21M, Anchored by Strategic Investment from Mitsubishi Electric
summary: Array Labs is working to provide high-quality 3D imagery on a global scale.
body_text: REDWOOD CITY, Calif., - Array Labs has raised $21 million in an oversubscribed strategic investment round, anchored by Mitsubishi Electric Corporation, one of Japan's largest defense and aerospace companies, with continued participation from Catapult Ventures, Kompas VC, and Y Combinator. As part of the financing, Array Labs and Mitsubishi Electric have entered into a partnership to develop and bring to market satellite-based airborne tracking services for mainly defense and security customers in the Asia Pacific Region. “Defense and intelligence customers have been asking for this capability for years, and this round lets us move faster to deliver it. An oversubscribed round anchored by a partner of Mitsubishi Electric's caliber is a strong signal that the market sees the same opportunity we do,” said Isaac Robledo, COO and cofounder of Array Labs. This investment follows Array’s Series A fundraise, announced in January 2026. Unlocking Continuous Understanding of Earth Traditional satellites are designed to image the ground. They periodically capture static, two-dimensional scenes: terrain, objects, infrastructure. They aren’t built to capture the motion, change, and activity happening around the world in real-time. Real-time monitoring of aircraft and ships has long been recognized as a critical capability gap. While a static image might tell you about a location at some point in the past, a continuous feed provides insight into how things are changing, where, and how fast. Traditional satellites cannot detect movement. Ground-based radar systems are constrained by the horizon line. Airborne ISR platforms have greater range, but are limited by cost, survivability, and operational constraints. Governments managing complex airspace, monitoring contested borders, and tracking activity across wide areas require a persistent orbital solution capable of continuously monitoring airborne and maritime activity anywhere on Earth. Array Labs is the difference between reacting to yesterday's picture of the world and understanding today's dynamic environment in real time. That shift changes what’s operationally possible: persistent awareness instead of periodic captures, patterns of life instead of isolated data points, and high-fidelity visualizations that show activity unfolding, rather than reconstructing it after the fact. The New Playbook Array Labs takes a fundamentally different approach to building radar satellites. Instead of relying on a single large, expensive satellite, Array builds mass-manufacturable radar satellites that fly in a cluster, operating together as one distributed sensor in orbit. By combining advanced signal processing algorithms, formation-flying satellites, and manufacturing techniques from modern telecommunications, semiconductors, and consumer electronics, Array can deliver higher power, wider coverage, and higher resolution systems at a cost and scale traditional space systems were never designed to achieve. The result is a continuously updated picture of the Earth that captures not just terrain and infrastructure but everything moving across or above it, including 3D and 2D imaging, naval and airborne monitoring, and space-situational awareness. No other commercial satellite operator offers this breadth of capability within a single integrated platform. Array has validated its core formation flying and multistatic technology, and earned competitive research and development contracts with DARPA, the U.S. Navy, and the U.S. Air Force. Array Labs and Mitsubishi Electric Partnership Mitsubishi Electric is one of Japan's largest defense and aerospace contractors, supplying advanced electronics, radar, and satellite systems to the Japanese Ministry of Defense for over half a century. In February 2026, it was awarded a contract to develop and manufacture Japan's next-generation defense satellite system. This partnership brings together Array’s transformative approach with Mitsubishi Electric's satellite system development capabilities, manufacturing infrastructure, and established relationships with defense, government, and other customers across the Asia-Pacific region. Together, Array and Mitsubishi Electric will bring moving object detection and tracking services to defense, security, and related customers. "We are very pleased to collaborate with Array Labs, which aims to demonstrate its game-changing AMTI technology. By combining the technological capabilities and maximizing the synergies of our two companies, we expect to strengthen our ability to respond comprehensively to customer needs in the security field," said Masahiko Arai, Executive Office, Company President, Defense and Space Systems, Mitsubishi Electric Corporation. “Mitsubishi Electric Corporation’s deep mission insights and defense relationships across Asia-Pacific make them an ideal partner. We’re excited to work together to turn space-based AMTI into an operational reality, helping humanity better understand the physical world,” said Andrew Peterson, CEO and cofounder of Array Labs. About Array Labs Array Labs is building a new way to understand the physical world. Based in Silicon Valley and backed by Y Combinator, Catapult Ventures, Kompas VC, and Washington Harbour Partners, the company is preparing to launch the world’s first coordinated fleet of radar satellites to deliver high-resolution, continuously updated intelligence about the Earth's terrain, infrastructure, and activity, operating day or night, through clouds, anywhere on the planet. For more information, visit www.arraylabs.io . About Mitsubishi Electric Corporation Mitsubishi Electric Corporation is one of Japan's largest and most established defense and aerospace contractors, supplying advanced electronics, radar, and satellite systems to the Japanese Ministry of Defense for over half a century. Headquartered in Tokyo, the company operates across defense, aerospace, energy, infrastructure, and industrial applications, and maintains partnerships with major defense primes across the United States and Europe. For more information, visit www.mitsubishielectric.com .

(NASDAQ: TEM), a technology company leading the adoption of AI to
body_text: Tempus Study Published in Nature Medicine Demonstrates Best-in-Class Performance of PRISM2 Across Diagnostic and Prognostic Applications August 4, 2026 PDF Version Tempus' multimodal foundation model offers diagnostic-grade precision for cancer detection and unlocks broader applications predicting biomarker status and patient prognosis CHICAGO--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 4, 2026-- Tempus AI, Inc. (NASDAQ: TEM), a technology company leading the adoption of AI to advance precision medicine and patient care, today announced study results demonstrating that PRISM2, a multimodal slide-level pathology foundation model developed in collaboration with researchers from Microsoft , can perform clinically important diagnostic tasks using simple prompts and can be leveraged for a variety of downstream applications. The results were published in Nature Medicine . PRISM2 outperformed or matched existing slide-level foundation models across a comprehensive set of diagnostic, biomarker and patient outcome prediction tasks. Additionally, when further tuned to specifically predict long-term outcomes, PRISM2 outperformed standalone models, including achieving high performance predicting colorectal cancer recurrence-free survival. "PRISM2 represents a true leap forward both in terms of scale and multi-modal AI capabilities," said Razik Yousfi, Senior Vice President and General Manager of AI Products at Tempus. “Our Pathology Foundation Models allow us to have a detailed understanding of tissue, unlocking clinical-grade precision and novel research applications capable of predicting patient outcomes and biomarker status. PRISM2 builds on this by aligning whole-slide pathology images with the language of clinical diagnosis through clinical dialogue training. It can seamlessly handle complex diagnostic and prognostic research tasks without requiring specialized fine-tuning, offering a powerful tool to advance precision oncology." As part of Tempus’ proprietary Pathology Foundation Models, PRISM2 turns routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) slides into deep biological insights. By combining large vision models built from pathology images with large language models, it unlocks diagnostic-grade precision in research involving cancer detection, biomarker identification and prognosis prediction. PRISM2 was trained on a diverse set of 2.3 million whole-slide images and 14 million diagnostic question−answer pairs derived from nearly 700,000 pathology reports, making it the largest multimodal slide-level pathology datasets to date. To support ongoing research, open science, and other non-commercial and non-clinical use cases, the full PRISM2 model weights are publicly available through Hugging Face at https://huggingface.co/paige-ai/Prism2 and https://huggingface.co/paige-ai/Prism2-survival . With one of the world’s largest libraries of multimodal data, and an operating system to make that data accessible and useful, Tempus provides AI-enabled precision medicine solutions to physicians to deliver personalized patient care and in parallel facilitates discovery, development and delivery of optimal therapeutics. The goal is for each patient to benefit from the treatment of others who came before by providing physicians with tools that learn as the company gathers more data. title: From Detection to Conviction: Forensic-Grade Gunshot Detection Evidence
summary: ShotSpotter’s Forensic Services supports public safety through forensic-grade gunshot detection evidence and expertise.
body_text: Camera-mounted microphones on fixed surveillance cameras serve a different function. They capture whatever sound happens to be near the lens at the time the video is being recorded, which makes them valuable for documenting the immediate surroundings. That design, however, has important limitations when it comes to recording gunfire. A fixed microphone is a single point of audio capture tied only to that camera, so the usefulness of the footage depends entirely upon the camera being close enough to the shooting in question and actually recording at the moment shots are fired. In contrast, ShotSpotter’s networked array captures the same gunfire from multiple locations, with recording triggered by the sound of gunfire itself rather than by motion sensors or timers commonly used by surveillance and doorbell cameras. Having multiple recordings also provides an important advantage when evaluating the sound of a shooting. While the recording closest to the shooting often provides the clearest representation of the sound and cadence of the gunfire, the surrounding environment can sometimes introduce echoes or other distracting sounds. In those instances, a recording captured from a different location may provide a clearer view of the gunfire itself. The advantage of a networked system also extends beyond detection and recording to the process of preserving and accessing the evidence. When gunfire is captured on a fixed camera, police must then take affirmative steps to obtain the video – often requiring a search warrant – and also must document the chain of custody for that recording. With ShotSpotter alerts, the ILS and audio are instantly available to the agency via the ShotSpotter app. The report and audio remain available on the app for 30 days and can be accessed through the historical database InSight thereafter. Upon request, SoundThinking can provide the ILS as a court-admissible Certified Business Record , accompanied by an affidavit that authenticates the record.

title: Do AI Image Tools Train on Your Data? What Enterprises Need to Know
summary: Which AI image tools train on your uploads, the 6-point checklist to run before you buy, and how Photoroom keeps enterprise catalog data private.
body_text: Some AI image tools train their models on the images you upload by default. Others process your images and leave them out of any shared model. This is the core of AI data privacy for enterprises, and that difference decides whether your product catalog becomes training data for a model that your competitors also draw on. Before you buy, confirm the vendor's default training setting, get retention and deletion terms in writing, and check for SOC 2 Type 2 and GDPR support. AI image tools now sit in the production path for millions of product listings, yet few buyers ask what happens to those images once the tool is done. In this guide, we'll review what training on your data means, what to check before buying an AI image tool, and how Photoroom handles your data. Table of contents Do AI image tools train on your uploaded data? Tools that train on your uploads vs. tools that don't What enterprises should check before buying an AI image tool Is your product catalog data private when you use an AI image API? How Photoroom handles your data Do AI image tools train on your uploaded data? Yes, many AI image generators use uploaded and public images to train their models. But training on uploads isn't a fixed rule across the board. It varies by provider and tool. Even within the same tool, it can come down to which plan or tier you're on. Because tools differ this much, it's risky to assume anything without checking. If preventing an AI from training on your images is important to you, always verify a specific tool's default setting and confirm whether you can opt out before committing to it or uploading data. The first thing to look for is transparency. Training on your images isn't necessarily bad, so what matters is whether a vendor is upfront that it's happening. When one hides it, that raises a fair question: does it treat you as a beneficiary, or as part of the product? What "training on your data" actually means General-purpose AI image tools build their training set from two sources: public images, and the files people upload while using the product. So the images you upload can do double duty: used once for your task, and again as training material the model draws on to shape outputs for other users. Vendors usually disclose whether they train on your images somewhere in their terms of service or privacy policy. Training on data is common enough across AI image tools that it's smart to treat it as the default when it comes to AI data privacy. For a consumer sharing a photo, the stakes are low. But for a business uploading its catalog, those visuals could end up training a model that competitors also rely on. This is the crux of the issue for many businesses. Why do AI vendors want to train on your images? Because it makes the models better. That is not a bad thing on its own, but it is worth understanding, so you can decide when you want it and when you don't. A general-purpose AI image model is only as good as the data behind it. The models most tools run on were trained on huge public datasets. Stable Diffusion's image generator, for example, learned from a set of more than 2 billion images scraped from the open web. Scale like that sets a model's general ability, but public data has a ceiling: it's messy, inconsistently labeled, and full of the wrong kind of pictures for selling products. Your product catalog is the opposite. Every image is clean, lit, labeled, and tied to a real product, a real category, and a real buyer. That is exactly the high-value, domain-specific data a model learns most from. So when a tool trains on your uploads, it isn't a trick. It's using good data to get better. The question for a business isn't whether training happens. It's who the improvement is for, and there are two cases: A shared model. Your catalog improves one model that every customer draws on, including your competitors. The gains from your data spread to everyone, and you can't pull them back. A model that's yours. Your catalog trains a model built for your products, your formats, and your brand rules. The same mechanism now works for you alone. So the answer isn't "never train on my data." It's "know who the training is for." When the improvement flows back to you, training is an advantage. When it flows to everyone else, it's a cost you handed over for free. Should you care if a tool trains on your images? It depends on two things: what's in the images, and whose model they train. For a consumer editing one photo, the honest answer is usually "not much." For a business putting its catalog through a tool at scale, it's "enough to make it a procurement question." Care more when: The images show unreleased products, new packaging, or pricing that isn't public yet. Bulk uploads reveal how big your catalog is or how it's structured. Your data trains a shared model your competitors also use. Visual style is part of how you compete, and you don't want it learned into a common model. Care less when: The images are already public, live on your storefront, your ads, or your marketplace listings. Nothing in them is time-sensitive or strategic. Training is opt-in to a model only you use, or you can switch it off. You're a small seller and the downside is low. The point isn't that training is dangerous. It's that only you know which side of that line your images sit on, so the choice should be yours to make. A good tool lets you opt out of a shared model in one setting, and opt in when training works for you. It also helps to keep the scale in perspective. Any single catalog is a small part of a training set that runs to billions of images, so ordinary product shots won't visibly shift a shared model, and images already public on your store or a marketplace may be in public datasets already. What doesn't get diluted by scale is a specific sensitive image, like an unreleased product or an unannounced price, or a distinctive style a model can pick up and echo. So scale is a reason not to worry about your everyday uploads, not a reason to stop caring about the few images that actually matter. What an uploaded product image can expose It's easy to assume a product photo is just a product photo. But a single shot often carries more than the product, and when a tool keeps your uploads, those details sit with a third party: Pricing: Price tags, discount stickers, or shelf labels caught in a shot can show pricing strategy, upcoming markdowns, or tiered pricing before they're public. SKUs and barcodes: Barcodes and internal SKU codes carry your internal naming and tracking systems, readable by anyone who can access the stored image. Catalog scope: Bulk uploads show a vendor how many products you carry and how your catalog is organized, including lines that haven't launched yet. Unreleased products: Pre-launch photos uploaded for editing or background removal put an unannounced product, packaging design, or seasonal drop in a vendor's hands before you've revealed it. None of this requires a data breach, or bad intent from a vendor. The moment a tool retains your uploads, these details live in someone else's systems, reachable by staff, a labeling step, or an incident. Training adds one more path, but a narrow one: a shared model can pick up a distinctive design or style and echo it in outputs for another customer, though it won't reproduce your exact prices or SKUs. Either way, the point is control. The real risk isn't that training happens, it's that your images are held and used without your say, with no audit trail to trace where they went. Encrypted product images Tools that train on your uploads vs. tools that don't AI image tools fall into two camps based on how they handle your data. Tools that train by default treat your uploads as training data unless you stop it. And tools that process only use your images to deliver the output you asked for and keep them out of any shared model. One thing to keep straight: a tool that keeps your uploads out of its shared model is not a tool that doesn't train. Every capable model is trained on a lot of data. The strong ones get there with public, licensed, synthetic, and consented data, giving you the option to opt out, and can still keep your specific catalog out of the shared pool, or train a model that's yours alone. So the real choice isn't between a sophisticated tool and a safe one. It's whether your own images end up in a shared training set. The two AI data privacy approaches, side by side An AI image tool's product page doesn't always tell you whether it trains on your uploads or only processes them. Often, you only find out once you read the terms and conditions, data processing agreement, or retention policy. It's worth confirming up front rather than assuming: if your uploads will train a shared model, you want to know before you commit at scale, since that decision is the hard one to reverse. What you're buying Who the improvement goes to Who it's good for Training on your uploads into a shared model Every customer of that model, competitors included Consumers and small sellers whose images are already public on a storefront or marketplace Processing only, no shared-model training (either by default, or via an option in settings) No one. Your images produce your output and nothing else An especially cautious business handling pre-launch products, visible pricing, or a look it competes on A custom model trained on your catalog You alone Teams running catalog-scale production against fixed brand rules What enterprises should check before buying an AI image tool Vetting an AI image tool isn't so different from vetting any data processor. Getting AI data privacy right here means confirming what happens to your content after the model has already delivered your output. Before you invest in an AI image tool, follow this checklist. The 6-point pre-purchase due-diligence checklist SOC 2 Type 2 . Ask for a current SOC 2 Type 2 attestation, which reports on how data security controls operated over a period of time rather than at a single moment. SOC 2 Type 2 is among the top recognized enterprise security standards, so a vendor without it or a sufficient alternative (such as ISO 27001) has a gap. GDPR compliance. Check that the vendor can satisfy GDPR requirements. That means having data protection by design and by default, a signed data processing agreement, a documented lawful basis for processing, and clearly defined rights for the people whose data is involved. Even if you're based in the US, this applies the moment EU customer or employee data enters the picture. Documented data retention and deletion. Get the retention windows in writing for images, jobs, and logs, plus a deletion process you can verify. If a vendor can't give you an end date for your catalog data, treat that as a red flag. A training opt-out, or no training on your data. Confirm whether your uploads train a shared model, and whether you can turn that off. If you represent an enterprise, it's best to have a contract that excludes your data from model training entirely. A published sub-processor list. A vendor that names its sub-processors shows you the full chain of who touches your data. Without that list, you can't assess downstream risk. No vendor lock-in. Check that you can move your workflow and data without rebuilding from scratch. A model-agnostic API and clean data export keep the switching cost low. Is your product catalog data private when you use an AI image API? Your product catalog data stays private on an AI image API if the vendor: Isolates your data. title: White-Tailed Eagles Return to Exmoor After Two Centuries in Historic Conservation Comeback
summary: White-tailed eagles have returned to Exmoor after more than 200 years. Discover how this conservation project aims to restore one of the UK’s most iconic birds and strengthen biodiversity.
